newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Siberian miners become slaves to their revolution.
newsitem.headline: Siberian miners become slaves to their revolution.

text.p: Several years ago mass protests by the miners of Siberia helped bring Boris Yeltsin to power. On Tuesday, they went on strike again, only this time to try to bring down his government.

Looking back bitterly on the heady demonstrations of 1989 -- which paved the way for the fall of communism two years later -- the miners now say the revolution that they helped bring about has turned them into slaves.
"In fact, we're worthless slaves, at least slaves get fed," said Oleg Kuslitsy, 34, a coal miner who has worked without pay since April.
He and thousands of other miners tapping the rich seams of coal running through Siberia's Kuzbass region, downed tools at the start of what they said would be an open-ended strike.
They are not the only ones. Teachers closed a string of schools on Monday and electricity workers in the region, home to more than two million people, plan a protest on Thursday.
"People want to eat and there is no money to buy food," said Viktor Korovitsyn, deputy chairman of the regional trade union federation.
Trade union officials said about 400,000 coal miners joined the protest across Russia. Interfax news agency said Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin could fly to Kuzbass to tackle the crisis.
The Kuzbass miners say they are not yet starving but barely know how to scrape by from day to day. "We live on the potatoes we grew in the summer," said one striking miner.
"And I sold my garage to a businessman. Other people sold their cars and motorcycles. And we live off the pensions of our parents, although they also do not get paid regularly."
More than 100,000 of the 260,000 Kuzbass miners joined the effort during the previous nationwide strike on November 5, making it one of the biggest one-day protests in the country.

On Tuesday, union leaders said 49 of the region's 76 pits stopped working completely or provided just enough coal to supply local power plants, while the local administration said only up to nine mines went on strike.
Whatever the figures, in 1989 such actions shook the foundations of the state. Today protests are unlikely to even bring pay, let alone the overthrow of the government.
Local officials say a tangle of interlocking debt between enterprises which has built up during chaotic market reform will take ages to unravel.
"There are mines that have been on strike for one or two months...but there is no money to pay. The state is bankrupt," said Anatoly Pronin, deputy governor of the Kemerovo region.
As for forcing political change, one look at Kemerovo's snowy central square on Tuesday was enough to see how it has become a dream harbored by a dwindling few.
Behind the vast statue of Lenin which still stands in front of the local government building, a small group of protesters stood in the winter sunlight, shivering in the freezing cold.
They numbered no more than 50. "People are tired of politics. Then (in 1989) they were interested. Now we are all divided. There is no solidarity," said Kuslitsy.
That goes not just for the region where many fear they will end up just hurting themselves by depriving themselves of vital heating and a future livelihood, but for Russia as whole.
"The miners say it is an open-ended strike, but they understand that it can't be. We would wreck the mine and any hope of reviving the industry," said the trade union's Korovitsyn.

"If the whole of Russia rose up, we could force the government out. But things vary from place to place. This is one of the worse regions. Others are better off. As long as it is just us and the Far East protesting there is not much."
